sections.heading: Complete sentences and fragments
sections.body:
A **complete sentence** has three things:

1. a **subject**: who or what it is about;
2. a **verb**: the action or state (*go, is, filed*);
3. a **complete thought**: it does not leave you waiting for more.

A **fragment** is a piece of a sentence that is missing one of these.

**Method: check for subject, verb and complete thought.**

- *The office near the plaza.* No verb: fragment.
- *Waiting for the bus.* No subject, and an -ing word alone is not a full verb: fragment.
- *Because the road was closed.* Words like because, although, if, when and after need a main idea after them: fragment.
- *Close the door.* Complete! In a **command**, the subject "you" is understood.

sections.heading: Run-on sentences
sections.body:
A **run-on** joins two complete sentences without the right mark or joining word. A **comma splice** is a run-on that uses only a comma: *The bus is late, we will walk.*

**Method: find the two complete thoughts, then check the join.** There are four correct ways to join them:

1. A period: *The bus is late. We will walk.*
2. A semicolon (;): *The bus is late; we will walk.*
3. A comma plus and, but or so: *The bus is late, so we will walk.*
4. A joining word like because or although: *Because the bus is late, we will walk.*

sections.heading: Parallel structure
sections.body:
**Parallel structure** means the parts of a list or a pair use the same form.

**Method: line up the parts, then match the forms.** Write the parts one under the other and compare them.

- **Lists:** *reading, writing, and counting*, not *reading, writing, and to count*.
- **Pairs:** not only … but also, either … or, both … and. What follows the first word must match what follows the second: *either call or **email***, not *either call or **an email***.
- **Comparisons with than:** *Walking is cheaper than **riding***, not *than to ride*.

sections.heading: Misplaced and dangling modifiers
sections.body:
A **modifier** is a word or phrase that describes something. Readers link it to the nearest noun.

**Method: put the describing phrase next to what it describes.**

- **Misplaced modifier:** the phrase sits next to the wrong noun. *She gave the cake to her friend in a plastic box.* (Is the friend in the box?) Better: *She gave the cake in a plastic box to her friend.*
- **Dangling modifier:** the doer is missing. *Opening the window, cold air came in.* (Did the air open the window?) Better: *Opening the window, I felt the cold air.*

Tip: after an opening -ing phrase and its comma, the very next noun must be the one doing that action.

sections.heading: Combining sentences
sections.body:
**Method: find the link between the ideas, then check the grammar.**

| Link | Use | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause and effect | because, so | *It rained, so the event moved indoors.* |
| Contrast | although, but | *Although it rained, the event went on.* |
| Same noun | who, that | *The man who called is my boss.* |
| Renaming | commas around the new name | *Ana, our cashier, is on leave.* |

A phrase that renames a noun, like *our cashier*, is called an **appositive**. Put it right after the noun it renames. Then reread your choice: no comma splice and no misplaced phrase.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.body:
- **Long is not complete.** A long group of words is still a fragment if the main subject has no verb of its own.
- **Commands are complete.** *Please sign here.* has an understood subject, "you".
- **The comma trap.** A comma alone never joins two complete sentences.
- **Same meaning, wrong form.** In parallel items, all choices say the same thing. Only one has matching forms.
- **The doer named too late.** *After checking the form, the request was approved by the officer* still dangles. The officer must come right after the comma.
- **Good grammar, wrong link.** In combining items, a choice can be grammatical but use the wrong joining word, like "because" for a contrast.

glossaryTerms.definition: A complete sentence has a subject, a verb and a complete thought.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Complete sentence – buong pangungusap; may simuno, pandiwa at buong diwa

glossaryTerms.definition: A fragment is a piece of a sentence that is missing a subject, a verb or a complete thought.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Fragment – putol na pangungusap; may kulang kaya hindi buo ang diwa

glossaryTerms.definition: A run-on sentence joins two complete sentences without the right punctuation or joining word.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Run-on – dalawang pangungusap na pinagdikit nang walang tamang bantas o pang-ugnay

glossaryTerms.definition: A comma splice is a run-on that joins two complete sentences with only a comma.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Comma splice – dalawang buong pangungusap na kuwit lang ang pinagdugtong

glossaryTerms.definition: Parallel structure means the parts of a list, pair or comparison use the same grammar form.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Parallel structure – pare-pareho ang anyo ng mga bahagi ng listahan o pares

glossaryTerms.definition: A modifier is a word or phrase that describes something. It should sit next to the word it describes.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Modifier – salitang naglalarawan; dapat katabi ng inilalarawan nito

glossaryTerms.definition: A dangling modifier is a describing phrase whose doer is missing from the sentence, so it seems to describe the wrong thing.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Dangling modifier – naglalarawang parirala na walang tamang tinutukoy sa pangungusap

glossaryTerms.definition: An appositive is a phrase that renames a noun, placed right after it, like "our cashier" in "Ana, our cashier, is on leave."
glossaryTerms.taglish: Appositive – pariralang nagbibigay ng ibang pangalan o paliwanag sa naunang pangngalan
